newsitem.title: SAUDI ARABIA: Saudi economy benefits from oil price windfall.
newsitem.headline: Saudi economy benefits from oil price windfall.

text.p: King Fahd and his advisers as well as economists and diplomats are again sounding bullish about the economy of Saudi Arabia, but the world's largest oil producer remains vulnerable to the uncertainties of international oil prices.

So far, those uncertainties are all in favour of the desert kingdom, which depends on oil for 75 percent of its revenues and is the major beneficiary of an unexpected multi-billion dollar price windfall.
The country's $40 billion budget announced in January assumed a price of $14 for each of the 8 million barrels of Saudi crude produced each day.

But the average price for this year has surged close to $18.50, giving Saudi planners a surplus of about $12 billion to factor into their calculations for dealing with a $4.9 billion 1996 budget deficit.
"The Saudi economy is strong and has firm bases," King Fahd said on the occasion of the Saudi national day this month.
Lower oil prices and the huge cost of the Gulf War produced cash flow problems for Saudi Arabia, which was the launch pad for the U.S.-led coalition that drove Iraqi invaders out of Kuwait in 1991.
But economic reforms are beginning to bear fruit, Finance and National Economy Minister Ibrahim Abdel Aziz al-Assaf told international bankers recently.
Gross domestic product growth was expected to be 6.2 percent this year, compared with 4.2 percent in 1995.
"For '97, clearly things depend on developments in the oil market, but we are also optimistic," he said at the annual meetings of the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank.

Assaf later told U.S. business leaders that Saudi Arabia was determined to press ahead with reforms. A stable currency pegged to the dollar and low inflation, estimated at 1.5 percent, made for excellent investment opportunities, he said.
Riyadh's ambassador in Washington, Prince Bandar, said the economy was improving and all indicators were heading in the right direction.
"I think we're seeing the end of the hard times," he told the U.S.-Saudi Business Council. The end of 14 years of deficit spending was in sight, he added.
The deficits began in 1983, when oil prices began to fall, and ranged up to $20 billion before narrowing toward the end of the decade. They shot up again after the war.
Saudi Arabia's budget spending is now under control, said Kevin Taecker, chief economist at Saudi American Bank.

"There's a strong commitment to fiscal discipline. This is now a $40 billion government, reduced from $60 billion over the last two years. That shows the strength of the economy," Taecker said in an interview. "Show me any other economy that can cut its economy by 30 per cent without a depression."

Taecker said the kingdom was building a clear vision for the future based on very realistic prospects for increasing the importance of the private sector while expanding the role of young Saudis in the kingdom's growth and development.
"The outlook for the Saudi economy into the next century is full of potential promise," he said. "What really gives confidence is that big parts of visions for the future are filled in."
Despite a period of worry when King Fahd fell ill nearly a year ago with what was reported to be a stroke, important parts of economic momentum after the war were still in place.

Taecker said Saudi negotiations for membership in the World Trade Organisation, which requires disclosure of trade figures, and an invitation to join the Bank for International Settlements, which reflected its leading position among the economies of the Middle East, were signs of progress.

Taecker expects the government to use the oil windfall to reduce the budget deficit, settle debts to contractors, help finance a $6 billion order for 61 airliners from Boeing Co. and McDonnell Douglas Corp. for Saudi Arabian Airlines, and fund new water projects.
"The economy is definitely in better shape," said a treasurer with another Saudi bank. Government debts to the agricultural and medical sectors had been partly paid.
But Saudi Arabia still has to build reserves, the banker said. "You can't run a car very far with the fuel gauge warning light on," he said.
